1:
The word Paul chooses for minister is not the usual one, and four of them stop to say so. Clarke gives the etymology: it means an under-rower, one who rowed on the undermost bench of a galley, and by extension any inferior officer — so that far from claiming to be heads and chiefs, the apostles rank themselves as junior officers employed under Christ, from whom alone they had appointment, work and recompense. Robertson adds that Paul uses the word here only, though it is common in the Gospels for the synagogue attendant and in Acts for John Mark. Ellicott presses the subordination hardest: the term is stronger than the one used a chapter earlier, implying not merely a man under one superior but a man in a still lower position, the officer whose business is to obey orders. Wesley takes the image devotionally, finding in the oar the pains every faithful minister takes in his Lord's work, and breaks off into prayer: where are these ministers to be found? Lord, thou knowest. Gill draws the practical consequence at both ends: they are not to be trampled on and treated with contempt, yet neither are they lords over God's heritage.

The second title lifts what the first had lowered. Clarke describes the office concretely: the steward was the master's deputy in regulating the family, providing food and serving it out in due season and quantity, receiving all the cash, expending what the household needed and keeping exact accounts to be laid before the master at set times. Robertson sets the rank precisely — a slave under his lord, yet a master over the other slaves — and quotes Lightfoot's scheme, that the Church is the house, God the householder and the members the household. Ellicott adds the detail that clinches the paradox: even the steward in a Greek household was generally himself a slave. Henry turns the pair of titles into a rule against both extremes. They are not to be overvalued, being ministers and not masters, stewards and not lords, with no authority to propagate their own fancies; but neither undervalued, since the Master's dignity puts an honour on them, and they are stewards not of common things but of divine mysteries, high-stewards in the kingdom of grace. Robertson agrees that the ministry is more than a profession or a trade: it is a calling from God for stewardship.

On the requirement of faithfulness there is one translation quarrel and one polemic. Ellicott would render the second verse, moreover here on earth inquiry is made in the case of stewards in order that one may be found faithful, and argues from the consequences: if the received English stands, it implies that the Church might prefer one steward to another on this ground, which is the very party spirit the epistle argues against. Robertson notes the manuscripts divide between it is sought and ye seek, an easy confusion once the two vowels were pronounced alike, and reduces the requirement to plain honesty in handling money, as in a bank clerk or any position of trust. Barnes explains why fidelity in particular: it is an office of trust, the master's goods are at the steward's disposal, and there is constant opportunity to appropriate them without detection. Calvin turns the same verse against Rome. Papists demand that whatever they teach carry the authority of law simply because they are called pastors; but Paul is so far from being satisfied with the title that even a legitimate call is not enough without fidelity in the discharge of it. Nor will he let honest teachers off: not every man who teaches the truth is faithful, but only he who desires from the heart to serve the Lord, Augustine having rightly given the hireling a middle place between the wolf and the good teacher.
3:
The phrase rendered man's judgment is literally man's day, and three of them work on it. Clarke argues from usage that the noun means a day appointed by a magistrate for trying a man, citing the psalm where the Lord laughs at the wicked because he sees that his day is coming, and the warning that the day of the Lord will come — and adds that the adjective carries the sense of woeful, as in the prophet's woeful day. Ellicott reports that some see a provincialism or a Hebraism, but thinks it likelier that Paul lived with the day of the Lord so constantly before him that the words became synonymous. Robertson keeps the contrast sharp, a human day against the Lord's day, and quotes the judgment that the Lord's day is the tribunal the apostle recognises and the human one he does not care to satisfy; what he denies is the competency of the court sitting at Corinth. Barnes guards the tone: Paul was not insensible to men's good opinion and neither despised their favour nor courted their contempt; he simply did not make it the principal thing. Wesley puts it in a line: his final state is not determined by his own judgment.

Chrysostom names the fault a disease and describes the symptoms. Along with all other ills there has come upon our nature a restless prying and unseasonable curiosity, which unlike other sins carries no pleasure but only punishment; and though we bear beams in our own eyes, we turn exact inquisitors of our neighbour's motes. At Corinth it had a particular form: religious men dear to God were ridiculed for want of learning while others brimful of evils were rated highly for fluent speech, and, leaving off to mourn their own bad ways, the congregation sat like magistrates trying causes and passing votes. Robertson supplies a pagan echo, quoting the emperor's wonder that every man sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on the opinion of others. Gill answers with the rabbinic maxim, be slow in judgment. Calvin marks the limit, since Paul cannot be setting himself above the Church's judgment as such: it is the part of a good pastor to submit both doctrine and life to it, and the sign of a good conscience not to shun the light of careful inspection. What Paul rejects is a judgment already corrupted, formed by men ravished with foreign masks.

The clause about knowing nothing by himself needs an ellipsis, and they agree on which. Barnes, following Grotius, Rosenmuller and Calvin, limits it to the apostleship: Paul is conscious of no unfaithfulness in that office, not of sinlessness at large. Calvin makes the point sharply: a man wholly unconscious of anything wrong could not have written the lament of the seventh of Romans; Paul felt sin and confessed it, but as to his stewardship his conscience did not accuse him. Clarke supplies a tag from Horace, the verb meaning to be conscious of guilt, as when the poet's man conscious of nothing never grows pale at a charge. Ellicott explains the obsolete English rather than the Greek: by here means concerning, a use he traces through the Old Testament and through a woman in Foxe accused of speaking evil words by the queen. Yet none of them lets a clean conscience settle anything. Robertson: failure to be conscious of one's sins is not innocence, and most prisoners plead not guilty. Calvin: what looks cleanest to us is filthy in God's eyes, so we must not measure his strictness by our own opinion. Hence the closing rule, in Lightfoot's words as Robertson gives them: do not anticipate the great judgment by a preliminary investigation, futile and incomplete. Barnes notes the praise then given means the sentence justly due rather than commendation; Clarke says some refer it to the apostles alone.
6:
Chrysostom explains the manoeuvre best, in two images. So long as harsh expressions were needed, Paul refrained from drawing up the curtain and argued as though he were himself the person addressed, so that no room was left for flying out in wrath; but when the time came for a gentler process he removes the mask. Then the sick-child simile: when a child out of health kicks and turns away from the physicians' food, the attendants call the father or tutor to take it from the physician's hands and bring it, so that out of reverence he may take it and be quiet. Robertson supplies the word behind the figure, a verb Plato and Aristotle used for changing a thing's form, and notes that Greek and Latin writers used the related noun for a rhetorical artifice — the same verb Paul later turns on the false apostles posing as apostles of Christ and on Satan as an angel of light. Gill enters the caution: these are not fictitious names, since the Corinthians really were divided and quarrelling over Paul, Apollos and Cephas.

Why these two names and not others is answered variously. Barnes reports Locke's view that nobody was actually set up as head of a party and the names are illustrative, but prefers the alternative: Paul names himself and Apollos to argue from the greater to the less, since if it was improper to make them heads of factions, how much more the inferior teachers. Clarke gives Bishop Pearce's paraphrase to the same effect, that Paul used his own name and Apollos's to spare naming the teachers actually heading parties, and guesses that Diotrephes was a ringleader. Ellicott adds the delicacy: had Paul written directly about Cephas and his admirers his motive might have been misread, and he and Apollos, as planter and waterer, layer of the foundation and builder, were the two whose exaltation would have seemed most pardonable. Calvin points the same way: those attached to Paul had not been so instructed and did not begin the parties. On the rule that follows, not to go beyond what is written, Robertson admits the idiom is hard to reproduce, an elliptical proverb with no principal verb, so one must supply either think or go; Ellicott takes it for not one passage but the whole tone of the Old Testament, which ascribes glory to God alone. Ellicott then makes the shrewdest observation here: it was not the teacher they puffed up, but themselves.

The three questions of the next verse divide them on how far they reach. Clarke keeps them narrow, addressed to one puffed-up teacher: if you have the knowledge you profess, did you not receive it from me or a fellow-helper who first preached here? He then says plainly that the general doctrine others build on the verse, though true, is no part of the apostle's meaning here — while warning against those who imagine themselves eternal objects of God's favour and others of his hate, for no reason they can give. Henry takes the maxim as broadly as it will go: nothing we have is properly our own, boasting is for ever excluded, and to glory in ourselves is to be proud at once of meanness, impotence and want. Gill runs the ladder of differences from the rest of creation through angels and beasts down to size, shape and countenance. Robertson says the question shuts out pride of intellect, blood, race, country and religion, and records that ten years before Pelagius the study of this verse and one in Romans crystallized the Augustinian doctrines in Augustine's own mind. Calvin turns it to church order: God assigned every member his own place, and if one leaps into another's office the body is undone. Barnes and Wesley close it: had God not interfered and made a difference, all would have remained alike under sin.
8:
That the three clauses are ironical nobody doubts, and Barnes uses them to defend the device: the passage is an instance of most pungent and cutting sarcasm, showing that there may be occasions when irony is proper, though rare — the standing precedent being Elijah on the priests of Baal. He also marks the climb: a man filled at a feast, then a man too rich to feel any want, then a man raised to a throne, beyond which there is nothing to reach for. Robertson sharpens the grammar to the same point, that the aorists used instead of perfects imply indecent haste, and reports the verdict that the Corinthians had got a private millennium of their own. Ellicott puts the weight on the word already and quotes Chrysostom, that piety is an insatiable thing and it argues a childish mind to imagine from the mere beginnings that one has attained the whole. Gill supplies the figure behind the first verb: as a full stomach loathes the honeycomb, so these men loathed the apostle's plain preaching, fancying themselves above it when they were still babes needing milk.

Clarke is the one dissenter, and he dissents from himself. He first gives Whitby's straightforward paraphrase, in which Paul means the Corinthians really are full and rich and flourishing without needing him; then says he is of opinion that a strong irony is intended, one which must have stung them to the heart. Both readings share the charge of ingratitude, which Calvin states most bluntly: Apollos and Paul are now esteemed nothing, though by their instrumentality the Lord conferred everything, and what inhumanity to rest complacently in God's gifts while despising those through whom they came. Wesley says the same domestically: they were like children who, having risen in the world, disregard their poor parents, the apostles being kept from self-complacency by continual want. Clarke turns it on the reader: it is not unusual for people to forget, if not despise, the men by whom they were brought to the truth, and take up with others to whom they owe nothing. Reader, he asks, is this thy case? At the wish that follows, Ellicott notes the irony is dropped and the words written with intense feeling, the word reign reminding Paul that the warfare of the Church militant will one day end.

The picture of the apostles set forth last is read against the amphitheatre. Clarke quotes Whitby on the two kinds of Roman show: in the morning men fought wild beasts with armour allowed them, but at midday the gladiators were brought out naked with nothing to ward off the assailant's sword, and whoever escaped was kept only for slaughter another day — men appointed for death. He sets Seneca beside it: in the morning men are exposed to lions and bears, at midday to their spectators, the victor detained for another slaughter and the fight concluding in death; the earlier fighting was mercy, this is mere butchery. Then his question: who at that time would have coveted the apostolate? Robertson adds that the rare word for the doomed is used in the Greek Old Testament of those thrown daily to the lions and by a historian of men flung from the Tarpeian Rock; the word for spectacle covers place, show and audience alike. Barnes reports Grotius taking the phrase ironically for the lowest condition, like that of beasts, as Tertullian rendered it, but prefers the arena. Calvin reads a triumph rather than an arena, prisoners led round for show then hurried off to be strangled, and admires that Paul was neither broken nor dispirited. Ellicott catches the stinging contrast: the Corinthians sit by criticising while the apostles do the fighting. Cyril alone turns the verse forward, to the martyrs who confess by being made a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men, martyrdom being itself a baptism.
10:
The three antitheses form one ironical figure, and Robertson supplies the anatomy: they refer respectively to teaching, demeanour and worldly position, the order inverting in the third so the sentence closes on a chiasm. Barnes calls it wholly ironical and exceedingly pungent, and adds what gives it force: the reverse was probably true, Paul being bold whatever opposition he met, while many of them were timid and time-serving, avoiding persecution and accommodating themselves to the prejudices of those they wished to please. Clarke reaches the same by a rule of thumb: the apostles were neither fools nor weak nor contemptible, and the Corinthians were not, morally speaking, wise and strong, so change the persons and the epithets will perfectly apply. Calvin heads off a misreading: some suppose Paul really abases himself and seriously credits the Corinthians with what he lacks, but the clause that follows refutes them, the whole being a concession made in mockery. Wesley catches the second half of the barb: they thought themselves wise, and had found means to make the world think so too.

Chrysostom shows the sentence working as argument, not complaint. Having said that God set the apostles forth last as men doomed to death, Paul now shows in what sense they are doomed: fools, weak, despised, hungry, thirsty, naked, buffeted, homeless, working with their own hands — the very marks, Chrysostom insists, of genuine teachers, while the rivals prided themselves on the opposites, wisdom and glory and wealth. He then puts the argument in Paul's mouth: the present is not a time of honour but of persecution and insult, such as we suffer; and if it is otherwise, if this really is the time of reward, then you the disciples have become no less than kings while we the teachers, first in line for the recompense, spend our lives in dishonours and hunger. Clarke keeps the theatre in view, quoting Philo on the treatment of the Jews at Rome: as if exhibited upon a theatre, we are hissed, most outrageously hooted, and insulted beyond all bounds. So the apostles are fools on Christ's account; had they walked after the course of this world, or the man-pleasing conduct of some at Corinth, there would have been no such cross to bear.

At the next verse the irony drops. Ellicott marks the change, from the sting of the word despised to a sad description showing how exactly it fitted Paul's position, not only in time past but at the hour of writing. Robertson counts what follows: ten verbs and four participles giving a graphic picture of his condition at Ephesus, several rare — a late verb for going scantily clothed, another for striking with the fist, a third found almost nowhere else for having no fixed abode, which one scholar renders simply that they are vagabonds. Ellicott prefers the reading that they are in want of sufficient clothing, and notes that to be buffeted is to be treated like a slave rather than a king, being without a fixed home a peculiar mark of degradation. Clarke puts the homelessness in the first person: mere itinerant preachers who, setting out in the morning, do not know where or whether they will get a night's lodging. Barnes turns it into a principle: poverty is no dishonour when produced by doing good, and Paul, who might have been rich, chose poverty for the gospel and was not ashamed to stand before princes in a worn-out garment. Wesley makes the picture a triumph: a man with an impediment in his speech and a person rather contemptible than graceful, appearing in mean and perhaps tattered dress before persons of the highest distinction, and yet commanding their attention. Gill notes it was not occasional but the constant course of their lives; Calvin, that Paul paints it so the Corinthians may lay aside loftiness and embrace the cross as he did.
12:
The manual labour gets several motives and one sting. Gill lists three: to supply his own necessities and those with him, to avoid burdening the churches, and to set an example of industry, though he had every right to claim a maintenance. Clarke adds the practical limit: this was necessary wherever no church had yet been formed, the people afterwards supplying their ministers according to their power. Ellicott places it at Ephesus, where the letter was written and Paul worked at tent-making with Aquila and Priscilla, and insists it was no pastime but hard and earnest work, made heavier by his generosity — as the farewell at Miletus shows, where he reminds the elders that these hands ministered to his necessities and to those with him. Robertson makes the same point culturally: Greeks despised manual labour, and Paul glories in it. Calvin finds the sting: Paul says not merely that he labours but that he works with his own hands, naming a mean and mechanical occupation; and in saying so he perhaps strikes at the false apostles, so effeminate and tender they could not bear to be touched with a little finger.

The three answering clauses read as instruction smuggled into autobiography. Barnes puts it exactly so: the main statement is that they were reviled and persecuted, while the responses are thrown in by the way to show how they bore it, so that in recounting his trials Paul was incidentally teaching the Corinthians how to bear their own. Robertson hears in the first clause almost Peter's language about Jesus, and behind both the command from the Sermon. Ellicott makes the contrast the point: a literal obedience to the Master, and the opposite of what the Corinthians would have done. Clarke turns it into an argument from experience: man is naturally a proud creature whose pride prompts him to repay insult with insult, and only the grace of Christ can make him patient under injury and render blessing for cursing. On the third verb they divide mildly. Barnes takes entreat to mean they besought their revilers to examine the gospel candidly, though he allows the alternative that they entreated God for them. Gill allows both, following the Syriac in taking it as beseeching the men themselves, and adds the manner: smooth words and soft language, not railing for railing. Wesley reduces it to a line: nothing but blessing.

The two words that close the passage are the chapter's strongest, and all of them go to one custom to explain them. Barnes gives the plain sense first, filth being what is swept from a house or cast away in cleansing, and notes that the Greeks used the term of victims offered to expiate crimes, men of ignoble rank kept for the purpose. Clarke supplies the ritual: in a public calamity they chose some unhappy men of the most abject character to be an expiation, kept them a year at public expense, then led them out crowned with flowers as sacrifices were, heaped the curses of the whole country on their heads, whipped them seven times and burned them alive, throwing the ashes into the sea while the people said, be thou our propitiation. Wesley knows the ceremony and reports that these very names were pronounced over the ashes. Robertson finds the second word in a formula used at Athens when victims were flung into the sea during a plague, and the first used of the scapegoat in Proverbs and by Epictetus of an expiatory offering of a worthless fellow — then hesitates, wondering whether Paul at Ephesus had heard such a cry raised against him. Calvin traces the preposition, which suggests the devoted men led round the streets so the cleansing might be more complete. Ellicott draws the conclusion the others leave implicit: the apostles are not merely the refuse of all men, but are so for the sake of others.
14:
Everyone notices the change of tone, and Robertson puts it in five words: the harsh tone has suddenly changed. Ellicott calls the abrupt shift from indignant expostulation to tender appeal characteristic of Paul, and adds that similar passages are nowhere found in the other apostles. Henry draws the pastoral rule out of it. The letter was written not with the gall of an enemy but the bowels of a father; in reproving sin we should regard the sinner's reputation as well as his reformation, since reproofs that expose commonly exasperate while those that warn kindly reform — to expose to open shame being the way to render shameless. Calvin faces the awkwardness others pass over: a father's chastisement is meant to make a son ashamed, everything Paul has written tends that way, and he will shortly say outright that he mentions their faults so they may begin to be ashamed. What he disclaims here is only the design of heaping public disgrace on them, since one who admonishes in a friendly spirit takes care that whatever shame there is stays between himself and the man admonished.

The word behind instructors gets the most effort. Clarke explains that the pedagogue was not the teacher but the servant who attended a child, had the general care of him and led him to school to be taught by someone else, and remarks that we improperly apply the English word to a schoolmaster. Robertson notes the term covers both offices, guide and attendant, and that these are the only two examples in the New Testament. Barnes and Ellicott make the contrast structural: whatever respect is due such men, the authority Paul claims is a father's, and Ellicott hears in the pairing the harsh severity of one office against the loving tenderness of the other. Calvin quotes an authority observing that the word has since come to carry an idea near contempt, the notion of a pedant assuming an authority not his own, whereas anciently it answered to a tutor who constantly attends his pupil and forms his manners — and who adds the sentence that settles it, that such a man may have some interest in his pupil but never the natural tenderness of a father. Gill takes the ten thousand as hyperbole for the false teachers, and wonders whether the Jewish members remembered the doctors and scribes who had also been called fathers.

Cyril alone puts the verse to a use outside the argument, citing it to prove that in Scripture the name father is not confined to the natural father: Paul was father of the Corinthians not by begetting them after the flesh but by teaching and begetting them again after the Spirit, as Job called himself a father of the needy, not having begotten them but having cared for them. Wesley presses the exclusiveness the other way: the claim shuts out not only Apollos his successor but Silas and Timothy his companions, and the relation carries an inexpressible nearness. On the call to imitation Clarke supplies the etymology, the word meaning an imitator in speech, manner or habit and giving us our word mimic; and he sets the ground plainly, that Paul lived for God and eternity, seeking neither glory nor ease, while the sowers of sedition were actuated by worldly motives. Barnes turns it into a test for ministers: a man should so live that he can without ostentation point to his own example and ask his people to copy it. Calvin enters the limitation without which the whole would be dangerous, drawn from Paul's own words elsewhere — follow no man except so far as he leads us to Christ. Ellicott calls it a family likeness; Robertson notes the imperative is continuous, keep on becoming imitators; Gill, that Paul, who might have used a father's authority, chose to entreat.
17:
Chrysostom begins from Paul's frustration. He was especially desirous of being present himself, knowing what a help his presence was and what a mischief his absence; and since it was not possible he corrects them by two substitutes, the promise of his coming and the sending of his disciple. The commendation attached to Timothy does double duty, showing Paul's love and preparing the Corinthians to respect him; and Chrysostom notices he is called faithful not simply but in the Lord, which matters, since if fidelity is high praise in worldly things it is more so in spiritual. Ellicott reconstructs the sequence. Timothy and Erastus had been sent ahead into Macedonia, and Paul did not expect Timothy to reach Corinth before this letter did; the earlier rumours had reached him before Timothy left, but Chloe's household brought worse news afterwards, and matters could not be left to grow until Timothy arrived, delayed as he would be along the way. Nor, Ellicott adds, would it have been safe to leave a man of Timothy's nervous and gentle temperament to face such anarchy alone. Robertson thinks Timothy had already gone and afterwards returned to Ephesus, and Barnes notes that even so his arrival was not certain.

What Timothy is sent to do matters more than that he is sent. Calvin isolates the two commissions: to recall to the Corinthians what they should have remembered of themselves, which is a tacit reproof, and to testify how uniform Paul's manner of teaching was in every place. The second was needed, he thinks, because Paul had probably been accused of assuming more authority over the Corinthians than over other churches, or of conducting himself differently elsewhere — whence the rule, that a prudent minister should so regulate his procedure that no such charge can be brought. Calvin also notes what qualifies Timothy: a witness needs knowledge of what he reports and fidelity in reporting it, and by calling him his own son Paul claims the first while stating the second outright. Henry presses the uniformity into a principle: Paul had not one doctrine for one place and another for another but delivered what he received, the truth of Christ being one and invariable, so that what an apostle taught at one time and place he taught at all. Henry adds the observation about memory that justifies the whole errand: those who have had the best teaching are apt to forget, and the same truth taught again, though it give no new light, may make a quicker impression. Wesley states the standard of comparison in five words, that Paul teaches no less by example than by precept.

The last verse names the inference they had drawn, and everyone reads it alike. Ellicott puts it as dialogue: some had been saying the apostle would never come, and the moment they heard Timothy was on his way they would take it as proof — he is afraid to come himself, so he sends Timothy. Barnes adds that Paul may have anticipated exactly this construction, and generalises: this is the haughtiness men assume when they suppose themselves in no danger of reproof. Gill and Clarke fill in the motive: they thought themselves safe through the apostle's absence and flattered themselves it would continue. Wesley credits Paul with foresight rather than report, saying he saw by a divine light the thoughts that would arise in their hearts. Calvin generalises it into a rule about the type: it is the custom of false apostles to take advantage of the absence of good men, so that they may triumph and vaunt without hindrance. He grants that wicked men sometimes do rise up openly with an iron front against the servants of Christ, but observes that they never come forward frankly to an equal combat, and that in preferring sinister artifices and indirect windings they betray how little confidence they have.
19:
The promise to come answers the taunt rather than predicting. Barnes states the logic: it is from no fear of them that he stays away, and to prove it he will come soon — a passage Bloomfield judged could not easily be paralleled for nerve and vigour, or dignity and composed confidence, even in Demosthenes. Calvin agrees the aim is not chiefly to terrify, since Paul presses on their consciences rather than threatening to thunder on arrival; however they disguised it, they knew he was furnished with divine influence, and were mistaken in raising their crests during an absence they assumed would be long. Gill enters the caution the others omit: this was said by way of threatening, not of prophecy, since it is not certain Paul ever did come afterwards. The attached condition draws further comment. Calvin sets it beside the rashness James derides, men planning ten years ahead with no security for a single hour, and grants we are not bound to such forms of words, though it is better to accustom ourselves to them, so that our minds are exercised in the thought that all our plans are subject to God's will. Robertson says it more briefly: it should represent one's constant attitude, though not always spoken aloud.

On the contrast between speech and power they divide over how much the second word carries. Barnes distributes it three ways: the miraculous power that founded the church, the Spirit's power in tongues and conversion, and the continual power needed to govern — holding a teacher who could show none of these unqualified. Clarke concentrates on the first, noting the word often means miracles outright, and denies that Christ's religion consists in human eloquence or even in doctrines, as against the mighty energy of the Spirit. Calvin turns the pair into a figure worth the whole passage. Outward gracefulness in teaching is like a body elegant and of beautiful colour, while the power is like the soul; it shows itself when a minister works by power rather than speech, placing no confidence in his own eloquence but furnished with spiritual armour — zeal for the Lord's honour, eagerness to raise Christ's kingdom, a desire to edify, the fear of the Lord, invincible constancy and purity of conscience. Without this, preaching is dead, whatever beauty it may have. The prating he sets against it is that of men excelling in gracefulness of speech while destitute of the Spirit's efficacy. Wesley reduces it to a sentence: real religion consists not in words but in God's power ruling the heart.

The closing question is read as a genuine choice put to the readers. Ellicott paraphrases: I am coming as a father in any case, but shall I come with a rod, meaning to use it, or as one comes when no fault of the child's need interfere with the unrestricted outflowing of his gentleness? The pathos of the last words shows which he would prefer, though the choice rests with them; and his love would be no love if, without any change on their side, it showed no displeasure where correction was needed. Robertson catches the image: a shepherd leans on his rod, and the pedagogue had one too, so they may have Paul as father or as pedagogue. Barnes notes the discipline was theirs to administer, and would devolve on him only if they refused it. Clarke supplies the background that made the threat credible: among the Jews those who did not amend after admonition were whipped in the synagogue, and the cases of Ananias, Elymas and Hymenaeus show that the apostles could sometimes inflict awful punishments, as the Corinthians must have known. Gill reports the Arabic and Ethiopic reading: how will ye that I come? Calvin ends where Barnes and Clarke began, complaining that whoever divided the epistles into chapters ought to have made this verse the start of one.
